title: Uniform centered negative contraction
statement: For every real $q\geq2$, there exists a real $c$ with $0<c\leq1$, and with $c=2/5$ when $q=4$, such that the following holds. For every probability space $(\Omega,\mu)$, every real-valued random variable $X$ in $L^q(\mu)$ with mean zero, and every $a\in\mathbb R$, the real-valued norms defined by converting the extended $L^q$ norm to a real number satisfy $N_q(a-cX)\leq N_q(a+X)$.
hypotheses_covered: There exists c with 0 < c and c ≤ 1
A measurable space Ω with a probability measure μ
Real-valued X with finite L^q norm, in the formal MemLp sense
Integral of X with respect to μ equals zero
replaced: For every $q\ge2$ there exists $0<c\le1$, with $c=2/5$ if $q=4$, such that every probability space $(\Omega,\mu)$, every real $X\in L^q(\mu)$ of mean zero, and every real $a$ satisfy $\|a-cX\|_q\le\|a+X\|_q$. Here $\|Y\|_q=(\int_\Omega|Y|^q\,d\mu)^{1/q}$.
